conflicts.point: Whether pre-market safety-gated certification and cryptographic provenance requirements are necessary guardrails or prohibitive barriers that delay life-saving interventions.

positions.stance: Insists that strict pre-deployment provenance and safety gating are mandatory to prevent unrecoverable harms because runtime telemetry cannot detect feedback-loop contamination.
Argues that static pre-market vetting creates fatal administrative bottlenecks and freezes flawed human baselines while patients suffer from treatable conditions.

conflicts.point: Whether real-time runtime telemetry and continuous out-of-distribution auditing can catch calibration drift faster than static review boards without falling victim to feedback-loop contamination.

positions.stance: Maintains that blinded out-of-distribution sampling and rapid telemetry updates catch operational failures and correct model weights faster than static review boards.
Asserts that runtime telemetry operating on data generated by prior algorithmic allocations suffers from recursive degradation and measures only how efficiently a system repeats its initial bias.

verdicts.conflict: Whether pre-market safety-gated certification and cryptographic provenance requirements are necessary guardrails or prohibitive barriers.
verdicts.rationale: The safetyist camp cites documented empirical findings, such as the 2019 Science study covering over two hundred million patients, to prove that historical data bakes systemic bias into algorithms. The opposing camp relies on general claims about administrative delay without similar large-scale documentation of harm.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Controlled trials showing that unvetted rapid deployment yields fewer allocation errors than pre-market certified systems would flip this verdict.

verdicts.conflict: Whether real-time runtime telemetry catches calibration drift faster than static review boards without feedback contamination.
verdicts.rationale: The safetyist position correctly identifies a recursive feedback loop where models trained on biased past allocations generate contaminated runtime data. The accelerationist claim that blinded sampling solves this issue lacks a mechanism to prevent the initial allocation bias from replicating.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Peer-reviewed demonstrations that out-of-distribution sampling successfully purges historical bias from runtime feedback loops would change the result.
